option_description: Controls whether the SMTP server requires TLS upgrades for all connections (enforced), advertises STARTTLS but permits plaintext fallback (opportunistic), or transmits entirely without encryption (none). This determines whether a network adversary can strip the STARTTLS advertisement to force a plaintext session.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires the opportunistic_tls_downgrade exposure when this value is 'opportunistic' or 'none' and neither DANE nor MTA-STS enforce is present. Because opportunistic mode allows an active attacker to strip the STARTTLS offer before the client sees it, any email carrying PII or credentials can be read in plaintext. Setting the value to 'enforced' causes the MTA to reject delivery rather than fall back to cleartext, blocking the downgrade path.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the Postfix main.cf file for the smtp_tls_security_level directive. A value of 'encrypt' or 'dane' corresponds to enforced; 'may' corresponds to opportunistic; 'none' means TLS is disabled.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: smtp_tls_security_level = encrypt  (or may, dane, none)

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Exim, check the tls_advertise_hosts and tls_require_ciphers directives in the main Exim configuration to determine whether TLS is advertised or required.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: hosts_require_tls = * (enforced) or tls_advertise_hosts = * without hosts_require_tls (opportunistic)

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use openssl to initiate an SMTP session and observe whether STARTTLS is advertised and whether the connection proceeds without it. If the server accepts MAIL FROM without STARTTLS, mode is opportunistic or none.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 250-STARTTLS in EHLO response; then successful TLS handshake. If the session proceeds without TLS upgrade, enforcement is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In SendGrid or AWS SES console, navigate to Settings > Mail Settings (SendGrid) or Configuration Sets (SES) and verify that the TLS enforcement option is set to Required rather than Optional.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SendGrid: Settings > Mail Settings > Enforced TLS | AWS SES: Configuration Sets > Event Destinations > TLS policy
how_to_obtain.expected_output: TLS policy shows 'Required' or 'Enforced' rather than 'Optional'.

option_description: Indicates whether DANE TLSA resource records are published in a DNSSEC-signed DNS zone for the domain's SMTP service. TLSA records cryptographically bind a specific TLS certificate or public key to the mail exchanger hostname, allowing sending MTAs to verify the server's certificate without relying solely on the public CA hierarchy.
security_impact: The Rego policy references dane_tlsa_configured as a condition in both opportunistic_tls_downgrade and missing_dane_or_mta_sts_enforcement rules. When false and MTA-STS enforce is also absent, both exposures trigger. DANE eliminates the STARTTLS stripping attack vector by ensuring that if a valid TLSA record exists and DNSSEC validates it, any certificate mismatch causes the sending MTA to abort delivery rather than accept a fraudulent certificate silently.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query DNS for TLSA records at the SMTP port on the MX hostname. A result confirms DANE is configured; NXDOMAIN or empty response means it is absent.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 3 1 1 <hex-certificate-hash> — at least one TLSA record returned with the AD (Authenticated Data) flag set in the full dig output.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the dane-smtp-check tool or check.sidnlabs.nl to validate DANE configuration end-to-end, including DNSSEC chain validation and TLSA record correctness.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: TLSA record validated successfully with DNSSEC chain intact.

how_to_obtain.instruction: On the sending Postfix MTA, confirm smtp_tls_security_level is set to 'dane' or 'dane-only', which activates DANE validation on outbound connections.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: smtp_tls_security_level = dane  or  smtp_tls_security_level = dane-only

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use swaks with DANE validation or mxToolbox DANE checker to confirm that a connecting MTA would successfully validate the TLSA record against the live certificate.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: TLSA record present with RRSIG signature and AD flag in response header.

option_description: Reflects the enforcement mode declared in the domain's MTA-STS policy file hosted at https://mta-sts.<domain>/.well-known/mta-sts.txt, as defined in RFC 8461. 'enforce' causes compliant sending MTAs to reject delivery if TLS cannot be established with a valid certificate; 'testing' logs failures but permits delivery; 'none' disables enforcement; 'absent' means no policy file or DNS TXT record exists.
security_impact: The Rego policy uses mta_sts_policy_mode in both opportunistic_tls_downgrade and missing_dane_or_mta_sts_enforcement rules. Unless the mode is 'enforce', the exposure triggers when DANE is also absent. In 'testing' or 'none' mode, MTA-STS provides observability but no actual blocking, meaning a downgrade attack proceeds unimpeded. 'absent' means the policy provides zero protection.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Fetch the MTA-STS policy file over HTTPS and print the mode field. A 404 or connection error means the policy file is absent.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: mode: enforce  (or testing, none; absent if curl returns 404)

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for the mandatory _mta-sts DNS TXT record. Both the DNS record and the HTTPS policy file must exist for MTA-STS to be active.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: "v=STSv1; id=<timestamp>" — if empty, MTA-STS is absent regardless of policy file.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the HTTPS MTA-STS Lookup tool at mxtoolbox.com (MX Lookup > MTA-STS) or dmarcian.com MTA-STS checker, entering the domain to retrieve the current mode and validate the policy file structure.
how_to_obtain.navigation: https://mxtoolbox.com/mta-sts.aspx — enter domain name and review mode field result
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy mode displayed as enforce, testing, none, or 'No MTA-STS policy found'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Manually verify the full policy file contents including version, mode, mx hostnames, and max_age to confirm the policy is correctly formed and not just partially deployed.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: HTTP 200 response with version: STSv1, mode: enforce, mx: <hostname>, max_age: <seconds>

option_description: Indicates whether the domain's DNS zone is signed with DNSSEC, providing a cryptographic chain of trust from the root zone down to the domain's resource records. DNSSEC is a prerequisite for DANE TLSA records to carry any security guarantee, and it protects MX record lookups from cache poisoning and DNS spoofing attacks.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers dns_mx_record_hijacking when dnssec_enabled_for_domain is false, because without DNSSEC an attacker can poison the resolver cache to return a rogue MX record, redirecting all inbound mail to an attacker-controlled server. DANE TLSA records are cryptographically meaningless without DNSSEC validation since an attacker could substitute their own TLSA record alongside a spoofed MX record. The missing_dane_or_mta_sts_enforcement rule also references this indirectly through DANE dependency.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check for DNSSEC DS records at the parent zone and verify the AD (Authenticated Data) flag is set on a signed query, confirming the full trust chain is valid.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DS record returned from parent zone; MX response contains RRSIG record and 'ad' in flags field indicating DNSSEC validation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the DNSViz or Verisign DNSSEC Debugger equivalent CLI tool to validate the complete DNSSEC chain for the domain.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'fully validated' indicates DNSSEC is correctly configured; 'insecure' or 'BOGUS' indicates absence or misconfiguration.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the online DNSViz tool (dnsviz.net) or ICANN DNSSEC Analyzer (dnssec-analyzer.verisignlabs.com) to visualize the DNSSEC delegation chain and identify any broken links or missing signatures.
how_to_obtain.navigation: https://dnsviz.net — enter domain name and click Analyze; review for green chain from root to domain
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All nodes in the delegation chain show green/valid status with no errors or warnings.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the registrar or DNS hosting provider's zone configuration to verify DNSSEC signing is enabled and DS records have been submitted to the parent zone.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Non-zero count of DNSKEY records indicates DNSSEC signing is enabled for the zone.

option_description: Describes the validity state of the X.509 TLS certificate currently presented by the SMTP relay on port 25, 587, or 465. Valid states reflect whether the certificate is issued by a trusted public CA, self-signed (issuer equals subject), expired (past the notAfter date), or issued by an unrecognized or private CA not in common trust stores.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers weak_or_expired_tls_certificate_on_relay for any value other than 'valid' (self_signed, expired, or untrusted_ca each have dedicated rule conditions). A self-signed certificate cannot be validated against a public trust chain, making MITM trivial if the connecting MTA accepts it. An expired certificate indicates the certificate lifecycle is unmanaged and the same server may present forged replacements without detection. Untrusted CA certificates allow an attacker with access to that CA to issue substitute certificates.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Connect to the SMTP relay using openssl s_client with STARTTLS and examine the certificate details including issuer, subject, and validity dates.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: issuer= and subject= differ (not self-signed); notAfter= is a future date; issuer references a public CA like DigiCert, Let's Encrypt, or Sectigo.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use testssl.sh to perform a comprehensive certificate validity check including trust chain verification, expiry, hostname match, and CA trust store membership.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Certificate trusted: yes; not expired; chain complete to trusted root CA.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the certificate expiry and self-signed status by fetching it directly and comparing issuer to subject fields.
how_to_obtain.command: echo | openssl s_client -connect <relay-host>:587 -starttls smtp 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -text | grep -E 'Issuer:|Subject:|Not After'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Issuer field references a CA organization name different from Subject. Not After date is in the future.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In the email service provider console (SendGrid, SES, Mailgun), navigate to the domain authentication or dedicated IP settings to verify the TLS certificate status and renewal date.
how_to_obtain.navigation: SendGrid: Settings > Sender Authentication > Domain Authentication | AWS SES: Verified Identities > DKIM and TLS settings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Certificate status shown as Valid with an expiry date at least 30 days in the future.

option_description: Categorizes the weakest TLS cipher suite that the SMTP relay is configured to accept during negotiation. 'strong' indicates only ECDHE or DHE key exchange with AEAD ciphers (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305); 'moderate' indicates CBC-mode AES without forward secrecy; 'weak' indicates broken algorithms including RC4, DES, 3DES, NULL, export-grade ciphers, or anonymous Diffie-Hellman.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers weak_or_expired_tls_certificate_on_relay when minimum_tls_cipher_strength is 'weak'. Weak cipher suites undermine the confidentiality guarantee of TLS even when the handshake completes successfully — RC4 is cryptographically broken, NULL ciphers provide no encryption, and export-grade ciphers are vulnerable to FREAK and Logjam attacks. The tls_protocol_version_cipher_weakness rule (referencing weak_cipher_suites_enabled) is the companion control; together they ensure cipher and protocol strength are both enforced.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run testssl.sh against the SMTP relay port to enumerate all accepted cipher suites and identify the weakest one offered by the server.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No weak ciphers listed. Output should show only HIGH strength ciphers with ECDHE or DHE key exchange and GCM or CHACHA20 modes.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nmap's ssl-enum-ciphers script to enumerate all cipher suites accepted on the SMTP port and their rated strength.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: All ciphers rated 'A'; no entries for RC4, 3DES, NULL, EXPORT, or anonymous DH ciphers.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the Postfix smtpd_tls_mandatory_ciphers and smtpd_tls_exclude_ciphers directives to determine what cipher classes are permitted or excluded.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: smtpd_tls_mandatory_ciphers = high; smtpd_tls_exclude_ciphers includes aNULL, RC4, DES, 3DES, EXPORT.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Exim, inspect the tls_require_ciphers directive to confirm weak cipher suites are excluded from the offered cipher list.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: tls_require_ciphers = HIGH:!aNULL:!eNULL:!RC4:!DES:!3DES:!EXPORT:!ADH

option_description: Indicates whether the sending or connecting MTA is configured to verify the remote relay's TLS certificate — including the certificate chain to a trusted CA, hostname matching against the MX record, and expiry — before proceeding with message delivery. When false, the MTA uses opportunistic TLS that accepts any certificate presented, including self-signed or expired certificates.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers weak_or_expired_tls_certificate_on_relay when tls_certificate_validation_enforced is false (via 'not input.tls_certificate_validation_enforced'). Without certificate validation, TLS provides confidentiality against passive observers but not against active MITM attackers who can insert their own certificate. An attacker on the network path can present any certificate — including self-signed — and the sending MTA will encrypt the message for the attacker. Certificate validation is required to make TLS meaningful against targeted interception.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the Postfix smtp_tls_security_level setting. Values of 'verify', 'secure', 'dane', or 'dane-only' enforce certificate validation; 'may' or 'encrypt' do not validate the peer certificate.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: smtp_tls_security_level = verify  (or dane, secure) and smtp_tls_CAfile points to a valid CA bundle.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Exim, inspect the tls_verify_certificates directive in the smtp transport to confirm certificate verification is active on outbound connections.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: tls_verify_certificates = /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt and tls_verify_hosts set to remote hosts.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test certificate validation enforcement by presenting an invalid or self-signed certificate to the sending MTA and observing whether it rejects or accepts the connection. Use testssl.sh to check what the MTA accepts.
how_to_obtain.command: openssl s_client -connect <relay-host>:25 -starttls smtp -CAfile /dev/null 2>&1 | grep -E 'Verify return code|certificate verify'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If validation is enforced, any invalid certificate causes connection rejection. 'Verify return code: 0 (ok)' with a valid cert only.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the sending MTA's mail log for TLS connection entries. Postfix logs the peer certificate verification result; 'Verified TLS connection' indicates validation is active whereas 'Untrusted TLS connection' indicates opportunistic acceptance.
how_to_obtain.command: grep -E 'TLS connection|Verified TLS|Untrusted TLS|certificate verification' /var/log/mail.log | tail -20
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Verified TLS connection established to <relay>: TLSv1.3 ...' confirms certificate validation is enforced.

option_description: Controls whether outbound email messages are cryptographically signed with DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) before transmission. When enabled, each outgoing message receives a digital signature in its headers that receivers can verify against the public key published in DNS, providing end-to-end message integrity protection.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'absent_dkim_message_integrity' exposure whenever dkim_signing_enabled is false or absent. Without DKIM signing, intermediate relay operators and network adversaries can modify message headers or body content — including injecting malicious payloads or altering PII — without detection at the receiving end. Additionally, the 'smtp_relay_hop_plaintext_leg' rule fires when plaintext_relay_hops_detected is true and dkim_signing_enabled is false, and 'replay_attack_on_smtp_session' fires when TLS is enforced but dkim_signing_enabled is missing, because DKIM timestamps and nonces help detect replayed messages.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check Postfix DKIM signing configuration via OpenDKIM milter integration. Look for the milter line referencing opendkim and verify the signing table is configured.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output should show 'smtpd_milters' or 'non_smtpd_milters' pointing to an opendkim socket, and opendkim.conf should show Mode containing 's' (sign).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Send a test message and inspect the received headers for a DKIM-Signature field to confirm signing is active end-to-end.
how_to_obtain.command: echo 'Test DKIM' | mail -s 'DKIM Test' test@example.com && dig TXT default._domainkey.yourdomain.com
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Delivered message headers should contain 'DKIM-Signature: v=1; a=rsa-sha256;' and DNS query should return a TXT record with 'v=DKIM1; k=rsa; p=<key>'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Google Workspace, navigate to the Admin Console DKIM settings page to verify the signing status and active key.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Google Admin Console → Apps → Google Workspace → Gmail → Authenticate email → Select domain → Check 'DKIM signing' status shows 'Signing emails'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Status reads 'Signing emails for this domain' with a 2048-bit RSA key listed.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Microsoft 365, review DKIM signing status per domain in the Defender portal.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Microsoft 365 Defender Portal → Email & collaboration → Policies & rules → Threat policies → Email authentication settings → DKIM tab → Select domain
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Domain entry shows 'Sign messages for this domain with DKIM signatures: Enabled' with a selector listed.

option_description: Specifies the bit-length of the RSA or Ed25519 cryptographic key used to generate DKIM signatures. This value determines the cryptographic strength of the message integrity protection — a 1024-bit RSA key is considered the minimum acceptable floor, while 2048 bits is the current recommended standard and Ed25519 (256-bit) is acceptable as a modern alternative.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'absent_dkim_message_integrity' when dkim_signing_enabled is true but dkim_key_strength_bits is less than 1024, treating weak DKIM keys as equivalent to no DKIM signing at all. Keys below 1024 bits are cryptographically broken and can be factored by well-resourced adversaries, meaning an attacker could forge valid DKIM signatures to make tampered or replayed messages appear authentic. Keys of exactly 1024 bits are technically functional but deprecated and should be migrated to 2048 bits.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the DKIM public key DNS TXT record and decode the base64 key material to determine bit length.
how_to_obtain.command: dig +short TXT selector1._domainkey.yourdomain.com | tr -d '"' | grep -oP '(?<=p=)[A-Za-z0-9+/=]+' | base64 -d | openssl rsa -pubin -inform DER -text -noout 2>/dev/null | grep 'Public-Key'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output shows 'Public-Key: (2048 bit)' or '(4096 bit)'; output showing '(1024 bit)' indicates weak key requiring immediate rotation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the OpenDKIM private key file to determine key bit-length directly from the key material on the mail server.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Line reads 'Private-Key: (2048 bit)' confirming the key strength in use for signing.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the nmap smtp-commands script combined with swaks to probe and then check DNS for key length using an online or local DKIM checker tool.
how_to_obtain.command: dig +short TXT default._domainkey.yourdomain.com | python3 -c "import sys,base64,subprocess; data=sys.stdin.read().strip().strip('\"'); key=data.split('p=')[1].split(';')[0]; f=open('/tmp/dkim_pub.der','wb'); f.write(base64.b64decode(key)); f.close()" && openssl rsa -pubin -inform DER -in /tmp/dkim_pub.der -text -noout 2>/dev/null | grep 'Public-Key'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Decoded key shows bit length; anything below 2048 should trigger a key rotation plan.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use MXToolbox DKIM Lookup to retrieve and inspect the published public key bit length without requiring CLI access.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Navigate to https://mxtoolbox.com/dkim.aspx → Enter selector (e.g., 'default') and domain → Click 'DKIM Lookup' → Review 'Public Key Length' in results
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Results display 'Key Length: 2048' or higher; a result of 1024 or lower indicates an at-risk key.

option_description: Defines the list of email message headers that are included in the DKIM cryptographic signature, specified via the 'h=' tag in the DKIM-Signature header. Critical headers like 'From', 'Subject', 'To', and 'Date' must be covered so that tampering with those fields after signing is detectable. Headers not in this list can be modified in transit without invalidating the DKIM signature.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers 'absent_dkim_message_integrity' when dkim_signing_enabled is true but 'From' is not present in dkim_signed_headers. The 'From' header is the primary identity field displayed to end users — if it is not signed, an adversary performing a header injection attack could replace it with a spoofed sender address while leaving the DKIM signature mathematically valid. Omitting 'Subject', 'To', or 'Date' similarly allows those fields to be altered without breaking the signature, enabling targeted social engineering or replay manipulation against PII-bearing flows.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect a recently delivered outbound message's DKIM-Signature header to read the 'h=' tag listing all signed headers.
how_to_obtain.command: swaks --to test@example.com --from sender@yourdomain.com --server localhost --port 25 2>&1 | grep -A5 'DKIM-Signature' || grep -i 'DKIM-Signature' /var/log/mail.log | tail -5
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DKIM-Signature header contains 'h=from:to:subject:date:message-id:mime-version:content-type' showing all protected headers.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the OpenDKIM signing table and configuration to find the SignHeaders directive which controls which headers are signed.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Output like 'OversignHeaders From,Subject,To,Date,Message-Id' confirms critical headers are protected; absence of 'From' in this list is a finding.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Parse the DKIM-Signature h= tag from a live email received at an external mailbox to confirm which headers are actually being signed in production.
how_to_obtain.command: echo '' | sendmail -bv test@gmail.com 2>/dev/null; grep -r 'h=from' /var/spool/mqueue/ 2>/dev/null || postcat -q $(mailq | grep -m1 '^[A-F0-9]' | awk '{print $1}') 2>/dev/null | grep -i 'DKIM'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: DKIM-Signature 'h=' tag lists: 'from:reply-to:subject:date:to:cc:mime-version:content-type:message-id'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use Google's Admin Toolbox 'Check MX' or the Gmail 'Show original' feature to inspect the h= tag in a sent message's DKIM signature.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Gmail → Open a sent message → More (three dots) → Show original → Search for 'DKIM-Signature' → Read the 'h=' field value
how_to_obtain.expected_output: The h= field should include at minimum: from, subject, to, date, message-id.

option_description: Specifies the mechanism used by the receiving mail infrastructure's DNS resolver to validate the authenticity of MX record responses. 'dnssec_validated' means the resolver enforces DNSSEC signatures and rejects unsigned or invalid responses; 'dnssec_opportunistic' means the resolver attempts validation but falls back to unsigned responses; 'none' means no validation is performed and DNS responses are accepted as-is.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'dns_mx_record_hijacking' when dnssec_enabled_for_domain is true but mx_record_validation_mode is 'dnssec_opportunistic' or 'none', and also fires unconditionally when mx_record_validation_mode is 'none' and DANE TLSA is not configured. Opportunistic validation provides false assurance — an adversary can perform a downgrade attack that strips DNSSEC signatures, causing the resolver to silently accept a spoofed MX response. Only 'dnssec_validated' mode closes this gap by refusing to accept unsigned responses for signed zones.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the BIND named.conf or resolver configuration to determine whether 'dnssec-validation' is set to 'yes' (enforced), 'auto', or 'no'.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'dnssec-validation yes;' or 'dnssec-validation auto;' in BIND confirms enforced validation; 'no' maps to 'none'; absence defaults to 'no' on older BIND versions.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Unbound resolver, check the dnssec configuration settings that govern validation behavior.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'auto-trust-anchor-file' present and 'harden-dnssec-stripped: yes' confirms 'dnssec_validated' mode; 'val-permissive-mode: yes' or absent trust anchor indicates 'dnssec_opportunistic' or 'none'.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Test resolver DNSSEC enforcement by querying a known deliberately broken DNSSEC domain; a validating resolver will return SERVFAIL.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A DNSSEC-enforcing resolver returns 'SERVFAIL' for this intentionally broken DNSSEC domain; a non-validating resolver returns an A record answer, indicating 'none' mode.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the mail infrastructure team or review cloud provider DNS settings to confirm whether resolvers used by the MTA are configured to enforce DNSSEC.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Review infrastructure documentation or ask: 'Does our DNS resolver used by the MTA enforce DNSSEC validation and reject responses for DNSSEC-signed zones that fail validation?' Check cloud DNS resolver settings (e.g., AWS Route 53 Resolver DNSSEC validation, Azure DNS DNSSEC settings).
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Written confirmation of 'dnssec_validated' mode with resolver configuration showing trust anchor files or equivalent enforced validation setting.

option_description: Controls whether STARTTLS or implicit TLS is mandated — not merely attempted opportunistically — on every SMTP relay leg throughout the message routing path, including internal MTA hops, third-party relay services (e.g., SendGrid, Mailgun), and smart hosts. When enforced, the sending MTA will refuse to deliver and queue the message rather than transmitting it in plaintext if the downstream server does not support or offer TLS.
security_impact: The Rego policy unconditionally fires 'smtp_relay_hop_plaintext_leg' whenever relay_hop_tls_enforced is false or absent, regardless of other controls. Email routing through multi-hop paths is particularly vulnerable because each individual relay leg is a separate SMTP connection — opportunistic TLS means a single non-TLS-capable hop in the chain results in plaintext transmission. The 'opportunistic_tls_downgrade' exposure also fires when STARTTLS enforcement is not in place and neither DANE nor MTA-STS provide compensating controls.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the Postfix smtp_tls_security_level parameter in main.cf, which controls outbound TLS enforcement for all relay connections.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'smtp_tls_security_level = encrypt' or 'verify' confirms TLS is enforced; 'may' means opportunistic (not enforced); 'none' means TLS is disabled — both 'may' and 'none' indicate relay_hop_tls_enforced should be false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Exim, review the transport configuration for the remote_smtp driver to check tls_require_ciphers and hosts_require_tls settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'hosts_require_tls = *' or 'tls_require_ciphers = ...' confirms enforcement; absence of these lines indicates opportunistic TLS only.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Microsoft 365 connectors, check outbound connector TLS settings in the Exchange Admin Center.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Exchange Admin Center → Mail flow → Connectors → Select outbound connector → Edit → Review 'Use Transport Layer Security (TLS)' setting — should show 'Always use TLS'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Connector shows 'Always use TLS' selected with certificate validation option; 'Use TLS when available' (opportunistic) means relay_hop_tls_enforced is false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use swaks to test relay behavior when TLS is unavailable by forcing a plaintext connection attempt against your outbound relay and observing whether it rejects or accepts the session.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A TLS-enforcing relay should respond with '530 Must issue a STARTTLS command first' or similar rejection; acceptance without TLS indicates relay_hop_tls_enforced is false.

option_description: Indicates whether any leg in the end-to-end email routing path has been observed or is configured to transmit messages without TLS encryption, as determined through analysis of Received headers in delivered messages, MTA transaction logs, SMTP TLS reporting (RFC 8460), or direct configuration review of relay nodes. A value of true is a direct finding of unencrypted transmission, while false indicates no plaintext legs have been detected.
security_impact: The Rego policy fires 'smtp_relay_hop_plaintext_leg' when plaintext_relay_hops_detected is true and dkim_signing_enabled is false — the combination is particularly dangerous because neither transport encryption nor message integrity protection exists for that leg. Even when relay_hop_tls_enforced is true, this attribute captures operational reality where a misconfigured relay or an emergency fallback may have actually transmitted messages in plaintext. Each unencrypted relay hop exposes full message content including PII and credentials to the relay operator and any co-path observer.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Scan Postfix SMTP client logs for connections established without TLS, which would indicate a plaintext relay leg occurred.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Zero results indicates no plaintext delivery events in the log period; any results show relay destinations receiving mail without TLS, confirming plaintext_relay_hops_detected should be true.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Parse Received headers from delivered messages to identify hops that lack 'with ESMTPS' or cipher annotations, indicating plaintext transmission.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Received headers showing 'with ESMTP' (without the 'S') or 'with SMTP' indicate plaintext hops; 'with ESMTPS' confirms TLS was used on that hop.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review SMTP TLS reports (RFC 8460) published by receiving domains to identify TLS failure events on outbound delivery attempts.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: TLS report files or log entries show delivery_summary with 'total_failure_session_count: 0'; any non-zero failure count indicates TLS could not be established on one or more hops.

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Google Workspace, use the Email Log Search in Admin Console to identify messages delivered without TLS and inspect their routing path.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Google Admin Console → Reports → Audit and investigation → Email log search → Filter by date range → Export results → Review 'TLS required' and 'TLS used' columns for discrepancies
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Rows where 'TLS used = No' in the delivery columns identify specific messages with plaintext relay hops, confirming plaintext_relay_hops_detected = true.

option_description: Indicates whether a valid SPF (Sender Policy Framework) TXT DNS record exists and is published for the sending domain. The SPF record enumerates the mail servers and IP ranges authorized to send email on behalf of the domain, allowing receiving MTAs to reject or flag messages from unauthorized sources claiming to originate from that domain.
security_impact: The Rego policy unconditionally fires 'missing_spf_dmarc_sender_authentication' whenever spf_record_present is false. Without an SPF record, any server on the internet can send email claiming to originate from your domain and receiving servers have no published policy to check against, enabling adversaries to impersonate your domain in phishing attacks or to inject spoofed email into the same channel used for PII and credential transmission. SPF absence also degrades DMARC effectiveness since DMARC alignment checks require either SPF or DKIM to pass.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query DNS TXT records for the sending domain and filter for the SPF record, which begins with 'v=spf1'.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns a record like '"v=spf1 ip4:203.0.113.0/24 include:_spf.google.com ~all"'; no output means no SPF record is published and spf_record_present should be false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nslookup to perform the same SPF record check across multiple DNS resolvers to rule out caching issues.
how_to_obtain.command: nslookup -type=TXT yourdomain.com 8.8.8.8 | grep 'v=spf1' && nslookup -type=TXT yourdomain.com 1.1.1.1 | grep 'v=spf1'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Both resolvers return the same 'v=spf1' TXT record; divergent results indicate DNS replication or TTL issues; no results from either confirms absence of SPF.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use an SPF validation tool like 'pyspf' or 'spf-tools' to not only confirm presence but also validate the SPF record syntax is correct and does not exceed the 10 DNS lookup limit.
how_to_obtain.command: pip install pyspf 2>/dev/null; python3 -c "import spf; result = spf.check2(i='203.0.113.1', s='sender@yourdomain.com', h='mail.yourdomain.com'); print(result)"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns ('pass', 'sender SPF authorized') for a valid record; ('none', 'yourdomain.com: No applicable sender policy') confirms spf_record_present should be false.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use MXToolbox SPF Record Lookup to check SPF presence and validate the record syntax against common misconfigurations.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Navigate to https://mxtoolbox.com/spf.aspx → Enter sending domain → Click 'SPF Record Lookup' → Review results for record existence and any syntax warnings
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Results show 'SPF Record Found' with the full record text and 'SPF Syntax Check: Pass'; 'SPF Record Not Found' confirms spf_record_present = false.

option_description: Controls the enforced DMARC policy declared in the _dmarc DNS TXT record p= tag for the sending domain. Values range from missing (no record) through none (monitoring only), quarantine (suspicious messages sent to spam), to reject (unauthorized messages blocked entirely).
security_impact: The Rego policy missing_spf_dmarc_sender_authentication fires when dmarc_policy is 'missing' or 'none', exposing the domain to email spoofing (T1672) and phishing (T1566). Without at least a quarantine policy, adversaries can send spoofed email appearing to originate from the legitimate domain, enabling credential phishing or PII exfiltration over the same trusted channel.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query the DNS TXT record for the _dmarc subdomain of the target sending domain and extract the p= tag value.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Returns one of: missing (no record), none, quarantine, or reject

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nslookup as an alternative on systems where dig is unavailable, then manually inspect the p= tag.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A quoted TXT string containing p=none, p=quarantine, or p=reject; empty output indicates missing record

how_to_obtain.instruction: Navigate to MXToolbox DMARC lookup at https://mxtoolbox.com/dmarc.aspx, enter the sending domain, and inspect the reported policy tag.
how_to_obtain.navigation: https://mxtoolbox.com/dmarc.aspx → enter domain → Review 'Policy' field in results
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Policy field shows None, Quarantine, or Reject; error shown if record is absent

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use the Google Admin Toolbox Dig API or a DNS-over-HTTPS resolver to programmatically retrieve the DMARC record for bulk domain assessment.
how_to_obtain.command: curl -s 'https://dns.google/resolve?name=_dmarc.<domain>&type=TXT' | python3 -c "import sys,json; data=json.load(sys.stdin); [print(a['data']) for a in data.get('Answer',[]) if 'dmarc' in a.get('data','').lower()]"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: JSON response containing the TXT record value with p= tag visible

typical_values: none (very common in legacy and misconfigured environments)
missing (common for subdomains and smaller organizations)
reject (mature security posture, required for compliance)

option_description: Defines the lowest TLS protocol version the MTA will accept for SMTP connections on both inbound relay and outbound submission ports (25, 587, 465). Enforcing a floor prevents negotiation of deprecated protocol versions that are vulnerable to known attacks.
security_impact: The Rego rule tls_protocol_version_cipher_weakness triggers when minimum_tls_version is none, tls_1_0, or tls_1_1, exposing connections to BEAST, POODLE, and other downgrade attacks exploiting weak symmetric (T1573.001) and asymmetric (T1573.002) cryptography. Additionally, smtp_credential_exposure_in_authenticated_submission fires when the version is tls_1_0, tls_1_1, ssl_3_0, or none even if TLS enforcement is otherwise set to enforced or opportunistic, meaning credentials transmitted during SMTP AUTH remain at risk.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use openssl s_client with STARTTLS to probe the minimum accepted TLS version on the submission port, attempting each deprecated version explicitly.
how_to_obtain.command: for ver in ssl3 tls1 tls1_1 tls1_2 tls1_3; do echo "Testing $ver:"; openssl s_client -starttls smtp -connect <host>:587 -$ver 2>&1 | grep -E 'Protocol|handshake failure|alert'; done
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Deprecated versions (ssl3, tls1, tls1_1) should show handshake failure; tls1_2 or tls1_3 should complete successfully

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the Postfix TLS configuration for the smtpd_tls_mandatory_protocols and smtp_tls_mandatory_protocols directives to determine the configured version floor.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Values such as '!SSLv2, !SSLv3, !TLSv1, !TLSv1.1' indicate minimum TLS 1.2; absence of exclusions indicates weak floor

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Exim MTAs, inspect the tls_require_ciphers and openssl_options directives in the main configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: openssl_options should include +no_sslv2 +no_sslv3 +no_tlsv1 +no_tlsv1_1; absence indicates weak minimum

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run testssl.sh against the SMTP port for a comprehensive TLS version and cipher enumeration report.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Report shows which protocol versions are offered; all versions below TLS 1.2 should show as NOT offered

option_description: Indicates whether the SMTP server accepts cipher suites that are cryptographically broken or deprecated, including RC4, export-grade ciphers, DES, 3DES, and CBC-mode ciphers without AEAD protection (e.g., AES-CBC variants vulnerable to BEAST or POODLE).
security_impact: The Rego rule tls_protocol_version_cipher_weakness fires when weak_cipher_suites_enabled is true, exposing intercepted SMTP sessions to decryption via attacks against symmetric cryptography (T1573.001) such as BEAST (exploiting CBC ciphers in TLS 1.0) and POODLE (exploiting CBC padding in SSL 3.0). Weak asymmetric key exchange ciphers also expose session keys (T1573.002), undermining confidentiality of PII and credential data in transit.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Run testssl.sh against the SMTP port to enumerate all accepted cipher suites and flag weak or deprecated ones.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: No output means no weak ciphers accepted; any matching lines indicate weak_cipher_suites_enabled=true

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use nmap's ssl-enum-ciphers script to enumerate accepted cipher suites and their strength ratings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Ciphers rated 'C' or flagged as weak indicate this attribute should be set to true

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the Postfix smtpd_tls_ciphers and smtpd_tls_exclude_ciphers directives to check if weak cipher categories are explicitly excluded.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: smtpd_tls_ciphers should be 'high' or 'medium'; exclude list should contain RC4:aNULL:eNULL:EXPORT:DES:3DES

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use openssl to explicitly test for RC4 cipher acceptance on the SMTP submission port.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: handshake failure or alert indicates RC4 is correctly rejected; successful cipher negotiation indicates weak_cipher_suites_enabled=true

typical_values: true (legacy MTAs and appliances with permissive defaults)

option_description: Specifies whether TLS is mandatory, optional, or absent for SMTP AUTH submission on ports 587 (STARTTLS) and 465 (implicit TLS/SMTPS). 'enforced' means plaintext AUTH is rejected; 'opportunistic' means TLS is offered but clients may downgrade; 'none' means TLS is not configured.
security_impact: The Rego rule smtp_credential_exposure_in_authenticated_submission fires when this attribute is 'none' or 'opportunistic', allowing SMTP AUTH credentials to be transmitted in cleartext or under downgraded encryption (T1586.002, T1071.003). An opportunistic setting is particularly dangerous as an active adversary can strip STARTTLS from the server greeting, forcing the client to submit credentials in plaintext without any session-layer warning.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the Postfix master.cf and main.cf for TLS security level settings on the submission service definition.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: smtpd_tls_security_level=encrypt indicates enforced; =may indicates opportunistic; absent or =none indicates not configured

how_to_obtain.instruction: Connect to port 587 and attempt SMTP AUTH without issuing STARTTLS first to determine if the server enforces TLS before allowing authentication.
how_to_obtain.command:
openssl s_client -connect <host>:587 -crlf 2>/dev/null & sleep 1; echo -e 'EHLO test.local
AUTH PLAIN
' | nc -q 5 <host> 587
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 530 Must issue a STARTTLS command first (enforced); server advertising AUTH before STARTTLS indicates opportunistic or none

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Exchange environments, review Send Connector and Receive Connector TLS settings via Exchange Management Shell.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-ReceiveConnector | Select Name, RequireTLS, AuthMechanism | Format-List
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RequireTLS=True indicates enforced; RequireTLS=False with TLS enabled indicates opportunistic

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft 365 or Exchange Admin Center, navigate to mail flow connector settings and review the TLS requirement checkbox for submission connectors.
how_to_obtain.navigation: Exchange Admin Center → Mail Flow → Connectors → Select submission connector → Edit → Security settings → Require TLS
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Require TLS' checkbox state reflects enforcement mode

typical_values: opportunistic (common default in many MTA deployments, insecure)

option_description: Controls whether the SMTP submission server refuses to process SASL AUTH commands when no TLS session has been established. This prevents credential exposure when a STARTTLS-stripping attack causes the client to fall back to plaintext authentication.
security_impact: The Rego rule smtp_credential_exposure_in_authenticated_submission fires unconditionally when tls_downgrade_protection_enabled is false (not input.tls_downgrade_protection_enabled), regardless of other TLS settings. Even if smtp_submission_tls_enforcement is set to enforced, the absence of this server-side guard means a STARTTLS stripping attacker (T1586.002) who modifies the EHLO response to remove STARTTLS advertisement can induce email clients to submit AUTH PLAIN credentials in cleartext over the hijacked session.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the Postfix main.cf for the smtpd_tls_auth_only directive, which is the canonical Postfix control for this protection.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: smtpd_tls_auth_only = yes indicates protection is enabled; = no or absent indicates it is disabled

how_to_obtain.instruction: Connect to port 587 without STARTTLS, issue EHLO, and inspect whether AUTH mechanisms appear in the capability advertisement.
how_to_obtain.command:
echo -e 'EHLO probe.test
QUIT
' | openssl s_client -connect <host>:587 -crlf -starttls smtp 2>/dev/null | grep -i auth; echo '---WITHOUT TLS---'; (echo -e 'EHLO probe.test
QUIT
'; sleep 2) | nc <host> 587 | grep -i auth
how_to_obtain.expected_output: AUTH mechanisms should NOT appear in the non-TLS EHLO response; presence of AUTH PLAIN or AUTH LOGIN without TLS means protection is disabled

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Exim, verify that AUTH is only advertised within TLS by checking the auth_advertise_hosts and tls_advertise_hosts settings.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: auth_advertise_hosts should match tls_advertise_hosts or be set only for TLS sessions; broad auth_advertise_hosts=* indicates protection is disabled

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to send AUTH PLAIN base64-encoded credentials to port 587 without STARTTLS and observe the server response code.
how_to_obtain.command: python3 -c "import socket,base64; s=socket.create_connection(('<host>',587)); s.recv(1024); s.send(b'EHLO test\r\n'); print(s.recv(1024)); s.send(b'AUTH PLAIN ' + base64.b64encode(b'\x00user\x00pass') + b'\r\n'); print(s.recv(1024))"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 530 5.7.0 Must issue a STARTTLS command first indicates protection enabled; 235 Authentication successful without TLS indicates disabled

typical_values: true (correctly configured in hardened Postfix deployments with smtpd_tls_auth_only=yes)
false (common default in many MTA configurations, insecure)

option_description: Indicates whether the SMTP server includes AUTH PLAIN or AUTH LOGIN in its EHLO capability response to clients that have not yet completed TLS negotiation. Advertising these mechanisms before TLS is established directly invites clients to transmit credentials in cleartext.
security_impact: The Rego rule smtp_credential_exposure_in_authenticated_submission fires when sasl_plaintext_mechanisms_advertised_outside_tls is true, directly exposing authentication credentials in cleartext (T1586.002). Unlike tls_downgrade_protection_enabled which addresses server-side rejection, this attribute captures the advertisement behavior: a server advertising AUTH PLAIN pre-TLS is actively signaling to clients (and attackers intercepting traffic) that plaintext credential submission is acceptable, facilitating credential harvesting via T1071.003.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Connect to port 587 without issuing STARTTLS, send an EHLO command, and inspect the full capability list for AUTH mechanism advertisements.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If AUTH PLAIN or AUTH LOGIN appear in the 250 capability list before TLS negotiation, this attribute is true; only STARTTLS should be advertised pre-TLS

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use swaks (Swiss Army Knife for SMTP) to perform a detailed EHLO probe without TLS and capture the server's capability advertisement.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: AUTH mechanisms listed in pre-TLS EHLO response indicate true; only STARTTLS in capabilities indicates false

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Postfix, cross-reference smtpd_tls_auth_only and smtpd_sasl_auth_enable settings to determine whether SASL auth advertisement is gated on TLS.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: smtpd_sasl_auth_enable=yes with smtpd_tls_auth_only=no means PLAIN/LOGIN are advertised pre-TLS; smtpd_tls_auth_only=yes prevents this

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use Python's smtplib to connect without TLS and enumerate the advertised ESMTP extensions including AUTH mechanisms.
how_to_obtain.command: python3 -c "import smtplib; s=smtplib.SMTP('<host>',587,timeout=10); s.ehlo('test'); print('ESMTP features:', s.esmtp_features); s.quit()"
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If 'auth' key in esmtp_features contains 'PLAIN' or 'LOGIN', attribute is true; key should be absent or empty pre-TLS

typical_values: true (misconfigured or default installations without TLS-gated AUTH)

option_description: Indicates whether the MTA is configured to require TLS for all SMTP sessions on inbound and outbound relay connections, preventing plaintext email transmission. When enforced, the server mandates STARTTLS completion before accepting message data or rejects connections that cannot negotiate TLS.
security_impact: The Rego rules replay_attack_on_smtp_session and email_traffic_metadata_leakage both reference smtp_tls_enforced. replay_attack_on_smtp_session fires when not input.smtp_tls_enforced, as plaintext SMTP sessions contain no session-layer uniqueness properties, allowing captured transactions to be replayed verbatim (T1672, T1071.003). email_traffic_metadata_leakage fires when smtp_tls_enforced is false or opportunistic alongside pii_bearing_email_flows_present, exposing envelope metadata (MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, headers) enabling traffic analysis (T1589.002, T1114.002).

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the Postfix main.cf for the smtpd_tls_security_level (inbound) and smtp_tls_security_level (outbound) directives.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: smtpd_tls_security_level=encrypt indicates TLS enforced; =may indicates opportunistic; =none or absent indicates disabled

how_to_obtain.instruction: Attempt to deliver a test message to port 25 without issuing STARTTLS and observe whether the server accepts DATA commands in plaintext.
how_to_obtain.command:
(printf 'EHLO test.local
MAIL FROM:<test@test.local>
RCPT TO:<postmaster@<domain>>
DATA
'; sleep 5) | nc <host> 25 | grep -E '^[0-9]{3}'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 530 Must issue a STARTTLS command first (or 220 greeting then rejection of MAIL FROM without TLS) indicates enforcement; 250 OK accepting MAIL FROM without TLS indicates not enforced

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Exim, check tls_advertise_hosts and tls_require_hosts directives to determine if TLS is mandatory or advisory.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: tls_require_hosts=* indicates enforcement; only tls_advertise_hosts without tls_require_hosts indicates opportunistic

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Exchange Admin Center or Microsoft 365, review Receive Connector security settings to confirm TLS is required for inbound connections.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-ReceiveConnector | Select Name, RequireTLS, PermissionGroups | Format-List
how_to_obtain.navigation: Exchange Admin Center → Mail Flow → Receive Connectors → Select connector → Security tab → Transport Layer Security (TLS)
how_to_obtain.expected_output: RequireTLS=True confirms enforcement; RequireTLS=False indicates opportunistic or disabled

typical_values: true (enforced, required for compliance frameworks such as PCI-DSS and HIPAA)
false (common in legacy relay configurations and open relay environments)

option_description: Specifies the duration in seconds for which TLS session tickets or session IDs are cached and accepted for session resumption on SMTP connections. Session resumption allows clients to skip a full TLS handshake by reusing previously negotiated session parameters. An excessively long window increases the attack surface for replay of captured session material.
security_impact: The Rego rule replay_attack_on_smtp_session fires when smtp_tls_enforced is true but smtp_session_reuse_window_seconds exceeds 3600 seconds (1 hour). A large reuse window means a captured TLS session ticket remains valid for replay for an extended period, allowing an adversary who obtained the ticket through network interception or server compromise to resume the session and inject or replay SMTP transactions (T1672, T1071.003). Setting the window to 0 disables session resumption entirely, maximizing forward secrecy at the cost of additional handshake overhead.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Check the Postfix TLS session cache timeout parameters for both inbound (smtpd) and outbound (smtp) directions.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Default is 3600s (1 hour); values above 3600 represent elevated risk; 0 means caching is disabled

how_to_obtain.instruction: Inspect the TLS session ticket lifetime configuration in the underlying OpenSSL or nginx-based MTA relay, particularly for session ticket key rotation intervals.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: ssl_session_timeout should be 1h or less; ssl_session_tickets off disables resumption entirely

how_to_obtain.instruction: Use openssl s_client with -sess_out to capture a TLS session, then reconnect with -sess_in after the configured timeout to verify whether the session is still accepted.
how_to_obtain.command: openssl s_client -starttls smtp -connect <host>:587 -sess_out /tmp/smtp_session.pem 2>&1 | grep -E 'Session-ID|Timeout|Reused'; sleep 3700; openssl s_client -starttls smtp -connect <host>:587 -sess_in /tmp/smtp_session.pem 2>&1 | grep -E 'Reused|New'
how_to_obtain.expected_output: 'Reused, TLSv1.3, ...' after the timeout period indicates reuse window exceeds expected limit; 'New, TLSv1.3' indicates session expired correctly

how_to_obtain.instruction: For Exim, inspect the tls_resumption_hosts setting and any associated session cache daemon configuration.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: tls_resumption_hosts absent or empty disables resumption; explicit host list with no expiry configuration indicates default OS-level timeout applies

typical_values: 86400 (24 hours, high risk, found in some appliance defaults)

option_description: Controls whether a deliberate mechanism—such as Postfix header_checks rules, Exchange Online transport rules, or an anonymizing SMTP proxy—actively strips or obfuscates SMTP envelope metadata (Received headers, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, originating IP addresses, timestamps) before messages transit external relay hops. This is distinct from passive TLS encryption; it specifically addresses whether routing metadata itself is suppressed or anonymized.
security_impact: The Rego policy triggers the 'email_traffic_metadata_leakage' exposure when pii_bearing_email_flows_present is true and envelope_metadata_protection_enabled is false, regardless of whether smtp_tls_enforced is set to 'opportunistic' or even 'enforced'. This means that even fully TLS-encrypted flows are flagged because TLS protects content in transit but does not prevent intermediate relay operators from reading SMTP envelope metadata. Without header stripping or anonymizing relays, sender-receiver relationships, communication frequency, and IP routing paths are exposed to every MTA in the relay chain, enabling traffic analysis attacks mapped to MITRE T1589.002 (Email Addresses) and T1114.002 (Remote Email Collection).

how_to_obtain.instruction: On Postfix-based MTAs, inspect the main.cf and any referenced header_checks or smtp_header_checks map files for rules that remove or rewrite Received headers and envelope metadata before outbound relay.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Lines matching '/^Received:/ IGNORE' or similar IGNORE/REPLACE directives in header_checks indicate active metadata stripping. No matching lines means protection is absent.

how_to_obtain.instruction: In Microsoft Exchange Online (Microsoft 365 Defender / EAC), navigate to Mail flow > Rules and review transport rules for conditions that remove or rewrite message headers such as 'Received', 'X-Originating-IP', or 'X-MS-Exchange-Organization-*' before external delivery.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-TransportRule | Where-Object { $_.RemoveHeader -ne $null -or $_.SetHeaderName -like '*Received*' } | Select Name, RemoveHeader, SetHeaderName | Format-List
how_to_obtain.navigation: Exchange Admin Center > Mail flow > Rules > Review each rule for 'Remove a header' actions targeting routing headers
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A transport rule with action 'RemoveHeader' targeting 'Received', 'X-Originating-IP', or similar headers confirms the control is active. An empty result set means no header stripping is configured.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Send a test message through the production mail gateway to an external mailbox you control, then inspect the raw message headers of the received email. Count and examine all 'Received:' headers to determine whether internal IP addresses, hostnames, or relay hops are exposed or have been stripped/replaced by the gateway.
how_to_obtain.command: swaks --to test@external-domain.example --from probe@yourdomain.example --server mail.yourdomain.example --port 587 --tls; # Then view raw headers of received message
how_to_obtain.navigation: In Gmail: Open received message > Three-dot menu > Show original; In Outlook: File > Properties > Internet headers
how_to_obtain.expected_output: If header stripping is active, Received headers should show only the external gateway IP/hostname with internal relay hops absent or replaced by a generic identifier. Presence of RFC-1918 addresses or internal hostnames in Received headers confirms protection is not enabled.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Interview the email infrastructure or security team to confirm whether anonymizing SMTP proxies (e.g., Anonymize.com relay, a dedicated anonymizing MTA tier, or a cloud gateway configured to collapse Received headers) are intentionally deployed as part of the outbound email architecture and whether this is documented in a data-flow or privacy control register.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Written documentation, architecture diagrams, or a confirmed change ticket demonstrating a deliberate privacy control for envelope metadata. Verbal confirmation without evidence should not be accepted as 'true'.

typical_values: false (most common — the majority of organizations do not implement header stripping and expose full relay chain metadata)
true (less common — typically seen in organizations with formal privacy programs, legal-sector email, healthcare, or deployments using dedicated anonymizing outbound gateways)

option_description: Indicates whether this email infrastructure is confirmed to carry messages containing Personally Identifiable Information (PII)—such as names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, financial account data—or credentials such as passwords, API keys, or session tokens. This attribute classifies the sensitivity level of the data flow and gates whether metadata-leakage and interception risks are materially significant for this specific email system.
security_impact: The Rego policy for 'email_traffic_metadata_leakage' requires pii_bearing_email_flows_present == true as a precondition before flagging any metadata exposure finding, regardless of TLS mode (none, opportunistic, or enforced). If set to false, the exposure is suppressed even when envelope metadata protection is absent. Setting this incorrectly to false on a system that does carry PII will cause the policy to silently miss a real exposure. When true and smtp_tls_enforced is 'none' or 'opportunistic', the risk is especially acute because both content and metadata are exposed to relay operators, enabling adversaries to perform traffic analysis (T1589.002) and remote email collection (T1114.002) against flows that carry sensitive personal data or credentials.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review DLP (Data Loss Prevention) policy match logs from your email gateway or cloud DLP solution (e.g., Microsoft Purview, Google Workspace DLP, Proofpoint DLP) for this mail flow to identify whether policy violations or alerts referencing PII classifiers (SSN, credit card, passport, credentials) have been triggered within the past 90 days.
how_to_obtain.command: Get-DlpDetailReport -StartDate (Get-Date).AddDays(-90) -EndDate (Get-Date) | Where-Object { $_.PolicyName -like '*PII*' -or $_.PolicyName -like '*Credential*' } | Select SenderAddress, RecipientAddress, PolicyName, RuleAction | Export-Csv dlp_report.csv
how_to_obtain.navigation: Microsoft Purview Compliance Portal > Data loss prevention > Reports > DLP policy matches; Google Admin Console > Reporting > Audit > Rules
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Any DLP rule matches for PII or credential classifiers confirm pii_bearing_email_flows_present should be true. Zero matches over 90 days on an active mail flow may indicate DLP is not configured rather than confirming absence of PII.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Review the data classification assessment or Records of Processing Activities (RoPA) for this email system to determine whether it is documented as a channel for transmitting personal data or credentials. Confirm with the system owner or data steward whether business processes such as HR notifications, account provisioning emails, financial statements, or password reset flows route through this infrastructure.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A data classification document or RoPA entry explicitly listing the email system as a PII or credential-bearing channel confirms the attribute should be true. If the system is documented as internal-only system notifications with no personal data, false may be appropriate.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Sample and inspect email content scanning logs or mail body analysis reports from the MTA or gateway to identify message patterns. Search mail logs for subject-line keywords or attachment types commonly associated with PII flows (e.g., HR reports, payslips, account statements, password reset links).
how_to_obtain.command: grep -iE 'password|ssn|social.security|account.number|reset|credential|payslip|w-2|1099' /var/log/maillog | awk '{print $7}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -30
how_to_obtain.expected_output: Significant match counts for PII-related keywords in message subject lines or envelope data confirm that PII-bearing flows are present. This is indicative only; content inspection tools provide higher-confidence confirmation.

how_to_obtain.instruction: Query your SIEM or email security platform API to retrieve DLP incident counts or content classification events for this mail flow over a defined lookback period, confirming whether PII or credential-classified messages have been detected in transit.
how_to_obtain.expected_output: A non-zero count of DLP or classification events from the SIEM API for this email infrastructure confirms pii_bearing_email_flows_present should be set to true.

typical_values: true (default and most common — virtually all enterprise email systems carry some PII through HR notifications, account management emails, customer communications, or password reset flows)
false (rare and only appropriate for fully isolated system-to-system notification pipelines carrying only non-sensitive operational alerts with no personal data or credentials)
